name: Tomas Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days start at the courthouse on Mercer Street, where I interpret Spanish and English for hearings, usually tenancy cases or small criminal matters. Afternoons I'm at my desk at home doing sworn translations: birth certificates, divorce papers, contracts for two law firms. I like the courtroom because a person is standing there who needs to be understood, and I'm the one who makes that happen. I do everything by hand with paper dictionaries and my own glossary, no AI at all.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Waiting, mostly. A hearing gets pushed back three hours and I sit on a bench in the corridor with Lucía, another interpreter, eating crackers. And the agencies wear me out, because every year they send a new rate card that's a bit lower and call it a market update. I still earn well because the sworn work pays more, but I can feel the squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. People kept saying translators were finished, and here we are, still standing in court every morning. I'd probably post something on the interpreters' association forum about not letting agencies use the hype to cut rates anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even a plateau isn't nothing for me. The agencies already push machine drafts and ask us to fix them for half the rate, and that wouldn't stop just because the hype faded. My court work is safe because a judge wants a sworn human, but the document side is already being nibbled at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do now: courts in the morning, sworn documents in the afternoon. I'd turn down the post-editing jobs, the ones where you fix a machine draft for less money, like I already do. I'd push the association to publish a minimum rate for sworn work, and I'd go to the meetings instead of just reading the minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a small knot underneath. I like my routine, and in this picture the routine survives. But the knot is the rate card, which keeps creeping down no matter what the technology does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned turning down post-editing jobs. How much of your income is that costing you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a tenth of what I could be earning, if I'm honest. Lucía takes them and she earns more than me some months. But I refuse to correct a machine's guesses for half pay. It feels like training the thing that's meant to replace me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the agencies kept cutting rates even in this world, what would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lean harder on the courts and the two law firms, because they pay a set fee and don't haggle. I've got more than a year of costs saved and my flat is paid off, so I can afford to say no. A lot of younger interpreters can't, and that's what makes me angry.

say: I'd say translators are **still standing** in court every morning, despite all the talk.
I'd warn colleagues online not to let agencies use **the hype** to cut rates.
think: I think the **document side** of my work is already being nibbled at, plateau or not.
My **court work** feels safe because judges want a sworn human interpreter.
do: Keep **courts in the morning** and sworn documents in the afternoon, as now.
Refuse **post-editing jobs** that pay half to fix machine drafts.
Attend **association meetings** and push for a published minimum rate for sworn work.
feel: He feels **relief** that his routine survives.
A small **knot** of worry stays about the falling rate card.
S0.quote: I refuse to correct a machine's guesses for half pay. It feels like training the thing that's meant to replace me.
fieldNote: He already turns down about **a tenth** of possible income on principle.
His paid-off **flat and savings** let him refuse work that colleagues must accept.
He frames rate cuts as a **fairness issue** for younger interpreters, not just himself.

steps.text: Keep the morning hearings at the Mercer Street courthouse
Push the interpreters' association to publish a minimum sworn-work rate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need rules. Courts, hospitals and police stations should be required by law to use a certified human interpreter, full stop. I'd sign every petition and I'd say so loudly at the association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my afternoons are gone. Birth certificates and contracts are the kind of writing and checking the card is talking about, and the law firms will run them through software and pay someone to stamp them. That's maybe forty percent of what I earn, gone over two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get serious at the association, maybe stand for the committee, and push for a law on certified interpreters in public services. I'd put more of my month into court work and ask the court office for extra sessions. I'd stop the small luxuries, like the weekly dinner out, and put that into savings, because I'd want two years of costs, not one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, more than scared. It's not that the machine got good, it's that nobody protected the people who did this work properly. And a bit tired, because I don't want to learn a whole new way of working at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you don't want to learn a new way of working. Would you ever try the AI tools, even to see what they do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I know that's stubborn. My view is that if I use the AI tools, I'm agreeing that a sworn translation can be a machine's guess with my name on it. I'd rather lose the document work than sign something I didn't really write.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your circle would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucía, oddly, even though she uses the tools. She's on agency work for most of her income and she has a daughter at home. If the agencies need one reviewer instead of five, she's one of the five.

I'd sign every **petition** and say it loudly at the association.
think: I think my **afternoon document work** will go within two or three years.

steps.text: Stand for the interpreters' association committee this spring
Lobby city councillors for a certified-interpreter law in public services
Ask the court office for three extra hearing sessions a week
Drop the weekly dinner out and save toward two years of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that governments let happen, and I'd mean it. I'd be out on the street with the association, and I'd be posting that every company using this owes something back to the people it replaced. Courts shouldn't hand a person's liberty to a machine, AGI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd lose almost everything within two years. Once a machine can interpret live as well as me, the courts will be under budget pressure to use it, maybe with one human on standby for appeals. The robots coming three years later mean nothing to me, because nothing I do is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything beyond rent-level basics straight away, even though my flat is paid off. I'd go all in on the association campaign to keep humans in court. And I'd start looking at work where a body has to be in the room, maybe as a support worker for Spanish-speaking families at the housing office, because those jobs at least have until the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor has gone. I chose translation because it felt human, and in this picture the human part is the first thing they decide is optional. I'd be lying awake doing sums, even with savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at support work. That's a big change for someone who doesn't like change. How real is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's real because the alternative is nothing. I'd hate the first months, and I'd probably complain to everyone. But a person who just got an eviction notice still needs someone next to them, and that's closer to what I love about court than sitting at a screen ever was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm fine for money for a while, which is true, and that I'm switching to something more stable, which is less true. My dad already thinks translation was a risky choice. I don't want to give him the satisfaction.

steps.text: Cut monthly spending to bills and food from the first month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and no excuse not to act. I'd be telling every politician who'd listen that we need a law now, while there's still time, that keeps certified humans in courts and hospitals. Online I'd be the annoying one posting the same petition every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like a slow version of the same ending for me. The document work goes first, probably in the first two years, and court interpreting holds a little longer because judges are cautious. Then it goes too, unless the law changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the switch earlier and calmer than in the fast one. I'd do a part-time course in social work in the evenings, paid from savings, while I keep the court mornings. I'd keep putting money aside and push the association to ask for a fund for retraining, paid by the companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less like falling, more like watching water rise. I'd still be anxious most days. But having five years means I could be angry and organised instead of just angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new things. Would you really sign up for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if it's people work and not screen work. I did my translation certificate at night while working in a café, so I know I can do the evenings. It's learning software I avoid, not learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing that would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first law firm sending me a polite email saying they've found a cheaper process. I'd print it and stick it on the fridge. Then I'd go and enrol.

I'd keep posting the same **petition** online every week.

Without a **law change**, it's a slower version of the same ending.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening social work course after the first lost client

Write to the local member of parliament about a certified-interpreter law
Save a fixed share of every court fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly, so let's do it fairly. I'd talk about apprenticeships for people like me into care work, and about making the companies pay for it. At the association I'd say we should plan, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years is most of my thirties, and that's a career. I'd probably still interpret in court for six or seven of those years. It's my forties I'd worry about, not next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as now and save hard, maybe aim to have three years of costs put away by 2030. I'd do the social work qualification properly, over two or three years part-time, so I'm ready to switch around 2032. I'd stay on the association committee to push for the retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, honestly. Still not happy, because I'm being told the thing I trained for has an end date. But ten years gives me a chance to choose my next work instead of grabbing whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having so much time make it easier to put things off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know that about myself. I'd put off the course every September if nobody pushed me. That's why I'd set a date and tell my colleague Lucía, so someone checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working with families in trouble, probably, in Spanish and English, in an office with real people coming through the door. Not rich, but useful. And still going to court sometimes, if they keep any humans there.

I'd call for **apprenticeships** into care work, paid for by the companies.
think: I think I'd still **interpret in court** for six or seven of those years.
My real worry is my **forties**, not next year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to get a law passed and no time to retrain. What would help is a rule that courts and hospitals keep certified humans, and a fund that pays for people like me to retrain into care work. Savings get me through a year or two, but they don't give me a new trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people on the other side of the table. When a tenant hears their case through a machine, nobody notices when they're confused or scared. I notice. I'd want someone to ask who notices after we're gone.

headlineQuote: When a tenant hears their case through a machine, nobody notices when they're confused or scared. I notice.
portrait: Tomas is a 27-year-old **Spanish–English** court interpreter and sworn translator who works without any AI tools.
His paid-off **flat** and over a year of savings let him refuse post-editing work on principle.
He blames **governments and AI companies** and pushes for a certified-interpreter law through his association.
He expects to lose his **document work** first and court work later, faster in the AGI pictures.
Across scenarios his plan shifts toward **social work** in two languages, if he has time to train.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's **no time** for a law or retraining.
whatWouldHelp: A law keeping **certified humans** in courts and hospitals, plus a company-paid **retraining fund**.
